passage:
Dear Ganga di,
You'll laugh at this. Our robotics team had to fill in a peer contribution form today, where each of us writes what percent of the work we did. I wrote 40%. Honestly, I thought I was being modest. I did the motor code and the wiring diagram, and I stayed back three evenings.
Then Prof. Iyer read the numbers aloud, without names. 40, 35, 40, 30. That's 145% of one robot.
Everyone went quiet. I'm sure Harpreet remembers her late nights on the chassis as clearly as I remember mine. I never saw her nights; she never saw mine.
Prof. Iyer said that from next week we keep a shared task log with dates. I grumbled, but I think it's fair.
Your brother,
Tushar

qa.q: What did the four contribution numbers add up to?
qa.a: They added up to 145% of one robot.

qa.q: Why did Tushar feel that writing 40% was modest?
qa.a: He clearly remembered his motor code, wiring diagram and three late evenings, while other people's hours were invisible to him.

qa.q: What will help the robotics team share credit fairly from now on?
qa.a: The shared task log with dates that Prof. Iyer asked for, so credit rests on records instead of memory.

qa.q: How might Harpreet see her own share of the robot?
qa.a: Harpreet probably remembers her late nights on the chassis just as vividly, so her own number feels right to her too.

grounding: A student realises every teammate claimed a big share of the work, adding to far over the whole, and accepts a written log.

passage: Chai stall, the night after our cultural fest. That's where it started, Sangeeta. I'm Lakshmi, and I ran the decoration team, five of us. We started saying who did what. I said I'd basically done the stage backdrop alone. Reuben said he'd done the backdrop. Farzana said she did the lights and most of the backdrop. Deepak said without his wooden frame there was no backdrop at all. We laughed, but it got tense. Each of us had been there for our own hours and missed everyone else's. Nobody was lying, exactly. This year, before we started, I made a shared sheet: every task, every name, every date, filled in the same day. Nobody argues now. Well, less.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi make before the team started this year?
qa.a: Lakshmi made a shared sheet with every task, every name, every date.

qa.q: Why did each person believe they had done most of the backdrop?
qa.a: Each of them was there for their own hours and missed everyone else's, so their own work felt like the biggest part.

qa.q: Why does the shared sheet help the team?
qa.a: Writing tasks, names and dates the same day replaces fuzzy memories, so credit is shared on facts and arguments shrink.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt when the others claimed the backdrop?
qa.a: Deepak may have felt his wooden frame was being ignored, since in his mind there was no backdrop without it.

grounding: A student recalls every decoration team member claiming the backdrop, and fixing credit with a written task sheet.

passage: I'm Nandini, and I share a hostel room with Sunaina, so I heard every chapter of her group's market survey. Monday night she said, "I'm carrying this whole project. I made the questionnaire." On Tuesday her teammate Kunal dropped by for notes and told me, quietly, that he'd done basically all the data entry, "like 300 forms." On Wednesday, in the mess, Ishita said she'd written the whole report and the others had just helped. I don't know who really did what. Maybe all three were right about their own parts and blind to the rest. On Friday Sunaina came back upset: their guide had asked each of them to write down their share, and together it came to far more than the whole. She sat down with a blank page and started a list, with dates.

qa.q: How many forms did Kunal say he had entered?
qa.a: Kunal said he'd done basically all the data entry, like 300 forms.

qa.q: Why might Sunaina honestly feel she is carrying the whole project?
qa.a: She lived through every hour of making the questionnaire but saw little of Kunal's data entry or Ishita's writing, so her part looms largest.

qa.q: Why is Sunaina's list with dates a good next step?
qa.a: A dated list shows who did what as it happens, so the team can agree on shares instead of each trusting their own memory.

qa.q: How does Nandini see the three different claims?
qa.a: Nandini doesn't pick a side, and thinks all three may be right about their own parts and blind to the rest.

grounding: A roommate hears three teammates each claim most of a project, until their shares add up to more than the whole.

passage:
Friday, late
The school library app launched today. Twelve hundred sign-ups in the first week. Everyone kept congratulating me, and part of me wanted to just soak it up.
Writing it honestly, since that's the point of this diary.
What I did well: pushed for the simple sign-in, and tested it with real students in two schools.
What was luck: the education fair happened the same week, and half our sign-ups came from there. I didn't plan that.
What I got wrong: I set the launch date too early, and Kashish had to fix the login bug on a Sunday.
Who I owe: Kashish, and Mrs Bhatia, who opened her school's computer lab for testing.
Sent Kashish a proper thank-you, naming the Sunday. Tomorrow in the review I'll say the fair part out loud too. Amma says I'm the first girl in our family to lead a launch. I want to do it straight.
Avni

qa.q: Where did half the sign-ups come from?
qa.a: Half our sign-ups came from the education fair that happened the same week.

qa.q: What does 'part of me wanted to just soak it up' show about Avni?
qa.a: Avni felt the pull to take all the credit, yet chose to write an honest account of skill, luck and mistakes.

qa.q: Why is Avni's plan for tomorrow's review a wise one?
qa.a: Saying the fair part aloud and owning the early launch date gives the team a true picture to learn from, which builds trust.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel on getting a thank-you that names the Sunday?
qa.a: Kashish would likely feel truly seen, because the note names the actual Sunday fix instead of a general thanks. 😊

grounding: A young professional sorts a launch's success into her own work, luck and mistakes, and thanks others by name.

passage: The seed-saving camp in Morena village drew ninety farmers, triple what anyone expected. That evening, at the block office, the district officer shook Saroja's hand. "Your idea, your success." Saroja smiled but didn't let it end there. "The idea was mine, and I'm glad I pushed for holding it after harvest," she said. "But the rain stopped the day before, which was pure luck. And I printed the leaflets only in Hindi, when half the women speak mainly the local dialect. Asif translated for three hours without a break. Karthik fixed the loudspeaker when it died at noon." Asif looked up from his tea, surprised. The officer nodded slowly and wrote all three names in the report. On the jeep ride back, Karthik asked Saroja to plan the next camp with him.

qa.q: How many farmers came to the seed-saving camp?
qa.a: The camp in Morena village drew ninety farmers.

qa.q: Why doesn't Saroja simply accept 'Your idea, your success'?
qa.a: She seems to want an honest record, taking pride in her idea while admitting the luck and the help she had.

qa.q: What could other team leads learn from Saroja's reply?
qa.a: Name your own good choice and your mistake, say what was luck, and credit helpers by their task, like Asif's translating.

qa.q: How does Asif react when Saroja names his work?
qa.a: Asif looks up from his tea, surprised, which suggests he didn't expect his three hours of translating to be mentioned.

grounding: A professional names her own good call, the luck of the weather and her leaflet mistake, and credits two colleagues.

passage: The ice-cream cart rang its bell at the gate of Sunrise Colony, and a dozen kids ran for it. Imran was first in line when Usha squeezed in front, her elbow knocking his arm. "Hey! You're so rude," he shouted. "Always pushing." Usha pointed at her building. "Mummy's calling me for dinner, I only have one minute!" Imran didn't hear that part. The next evening Imran was the one running late for his tabla class. He shoved past two kids at the cart, grabbed his cone and ran. "Sorry, sorry, I'm late!" he called over his shoulder, feeling perfectly reasonable. That night he told his father, "Usha pushes because she's rude. I only pushed because I had tabla." His father looked at him for a long moment.

qa.q: Why was Imran in a hurry the next evening?
qa.a: Imran was running late for his tabla class.

qa.q: Why did Imran feel perfectly reasonable shoving past the kids?
qa.a: He knew all about his late tabla class, so his push felt explained, while Usha's reason never reached him.

qa.q: What could Imran's father ask to help him?
qa.a: His father could ask, 'What did Usha say when she pushed?' so Imran remembers that her mummy was calling her too.

qa.q: How might the two kids Imran shoved see him?
qa.a: They only saw a boy pushing past them, so they might call him rude, just as Imran called Usha.

grounding: A boy excuses his own push by his hurry but calls a girl's push rude, ignoring that she was in a hurry too.

passage:
"You pushed me off the swing!" Noor said, brushing sand off her knees.
"I didn't push. I just needed a turn fast. The bell was about to ring," said Thomas.
"So? Yesterday when Kiran pushed you off the slide, you said he was a bully."
"Because he is. He pushes everyone."
"And you pushed me."
"That's different. I had a reason."
"Maybe Kiran had a reason too."
"Like what?"
Noor shrugged. "Maybe the bell was about to ring for him too."
Thomas kicked at the sand. "His reason is he's mean."
"And your reason is the bell?"
"Yes."
Noor climbed back onto the swing. "Then I'm keeping it, because the bell hasn't rung."

qa.q: Why does Thomas say Noor was pushed off the swing?
qa.a: Thomas says the push was only about needing a turn fast because the bell was about to ring.

qa.q: Why does Thomas think that push is different from Kiran's?
qa.a: Thomas feels that rush from inside, so that push has a reason, while Kiran is only seen from outside, so Kiran's push gets called mean.

qa.q: What could Thomas try when he wants to call someone a bully?
qa.a: Thomas could ask what reason Kiran might have had, just as Thomas had one.

qa.q: How does Noor see the two pushes?
qa.a: Noor sees them as the same kind of push and wonders why only Thomas gets to have a reason.

grounding: A child says their own push came from being rushed but a classmate's push came from being mean.

passage: I'm Ronak, and this happened in the morning assembly line. Shreya pushed me from behind and I nearly fell on the boy in front. I told Manjula Miss, "Shreya is rude. She always pushes." Then, when the line moved to our classroom, I pushed Deepu so I could get the window seat before anyone else. Manjula Miss said, "Good boys don't push, Ronak." I said I was in a hurry because my bag was so heavy. Later I found out Shreya had been pushed by the big boys behind her. I felt a bit silly. My push had a reason, but I never asked about hers. Now I think maybe she had a reason too.

qa.q: Why did Ronak push Deepu?
qa.a: He pushed Deepu so he could get the window seat before anyone else.

qa.q: How did Ronak feel after learning why Shreya pushed?
qa.a: He felt a bit silly, because his own push had a reason but he never asked about hers.

qa.q: What would you advise Ronak when someone pushes him in the line?
qa.a: Before calling them rude, he could look behind them or ask what happened, since someone might be pushing them too.

qa.q: How might Deepu feel about being pushed for the window seat?
qa.a: Deepu might think Ronak is rude, just as Ronak thought about Shreya, because Deepu can't see the heavy bag.

grounding: A boy blames a classmate's rudeness for her push while excusing his own push by his hurry.

passage: At nine in the evening, in a second-floor flat in Hyderabad, the argument started over the Wi-Fi password. Harsh's mother, Uma, had changed it because his marks had dipped. "You can't just control my life!" Harsh shouted. "I have three tests this week, I'm stressed out!" Uma's voice rose too. "Don't shout at me! You're being disrespectful!" Harsh slammed his door. Inside, he thought: she shouts because she likes being in charge; I shout because I'm under pressure. In the kitchen, Uma told his sister Jaya, "He shouts because he's become arrogant. I only raised my voice because I'm worried about his marks and I had a terrible day at the office." Jaya, who'd heard both sides, just kept chopping onions.

qa.q: Why had Uma changed the Wi-Fi password?
qa.a: Uma had changed it because Harsh's marks had dipped.

qa.q: Why does Harsh think his own shouting is different from his mother's?
qa.a: Harsh thinks he shouts because he's under pressure from three tests, but that Uma shouts because she likes being in charge.

qa.q: What could Harsh and Uma try once they have both calmed down?
qa.a: Each could say what their own day was like before discussing the password, so both sets of pressure become visible.

qa.q: How is Jaya's view different from Harsh's and Uma's?
qa.a: Jaya has heard both sides, so she can see that each explains their own shouting by stress and the other's by character.

grounding: A teenage son and his mother each excuse their own shouting by stress while reading the other's as arrogance or control.

passage:
"Rayan, it's eleven. Phone. Now."
"Ammi, I'm finishing the physics worksheet!"
"You said that an hour ago."
"Because you keep interrupting! Why are you always shouting?"
"I'm shouting? You're the one yelling!"
"I'm yelling because I've got a test tomorrow and I'm stressed! You're yelling because you want to control everything."
Afreen put her hand on the doorframe. "Control? I'm yelling because I'm tired and worried you'll be exhausted tomorrow. You're yelling because you've become rude, young man."
"I'm not rude, I'm stressed!"
"And I'm not controlling, I'm worried!"
They both stopped. The fan clicked overhead.
"So we're both saying the same thing," Rayan muttered.
Afreen almost smiled. "Finish the worksheet. Ten minutes."

qa.q: What time is it when Afreen asks for the phone?
qa.a: It's eleven.

qa.q: Why does Rayan believe his own yelling is justified?
qa.a: He feels the stress of tomorrow's test from the inside, so his yelling seems caused by pressure, while Ammi's seems to come from wanting control.

qa.q: What could Rayan and Afreen do earlier next time?
qa.a: They could agree on a phone time before the evening starts, and each say 'I'm stressed' or 'I'm worried' before voices rise.

qa.q: How does Afreen explain her own yelling?
qa.a: Afreen says she is yelling because she is tired and worried he'll be exhausted, not because she wants control.

grounding: A teenage son and his mother each blame their own shouting on stress or worry and the other's on control or rudeness.

passage: I'm Sachin, and last Sunday I had a huge fight with my father about the cricket academy. He said the fees were too much this year. I said, loudly, that he never supports anything I love. He said, louder, that I don't understand money. Then I shouted that he just likes saying no. Later, lying on my bed, I was sure I'd only shouted because I'd had a terrible week at school and the selection trials are close. And he'd shouted because he's controlling. My mother, Chandrika, came in and said something I keep thinking about: "Your father thinks you shouted because you're a spoilt boy, and that he shouted because the shop had a bad month." I hadn't known about the shop. He hadn't known about my week.

qa.q: Why did Sachin's father say no to the academy?
qa.a: He said the fees were too much this year.

qa.q: Why was Sachin so sure his own shouting was different?
qa.a: He knew about his terrible week and the close selection trials, so his anger felt explained, while his father's seemed like pure control.

qa.q: What could Sachin try in the next talk with his father?
qa.a: He could share how his week went and ask about the shop's bad month, so both of them see the other's pressure.

qa.q: How does Sachin's father see the same fight?
qa.a: His father thinks Sachin shouted because he is a spoilt boy, while his own shouting came from the shop's bad month.

grounding: A teenager explains his own shouting by a bad week but his father's by control, while the father sees it the opposite way.

passage: Liam sat on the steps outside his student flat in Leeds, still angry. Emeka had played loud music at midnight again, the night before Liam's statistics exam. Liam opened a notes page on his phone and made himself write it as if it were his friend Callum's story: "Callum's flatmate played music late before Callum's exam." Reading it that way, he thought: Callum should just knock and ask, calmly. Then he tried Emeka's seat. Emeka had started night shifts at the warehouse; midnight was his only time to unwind. He'd probably not seen the exam date on the kitchen calendar, half-hidden behind the takeaway menus. And Liam himself had banged the front door at seven every morning that week for early lectures. He went inside and knocked on Emeka's door with two mugs of tea.

qa.q: Where did Liam sit while he was still angry?
qa.a: Liam sat on the steps outside his student flat in Leeds.

qa.q: What did writing it as Callum's story change in Liam's thinking?
qa.a: Seen from a distance, the calm answer, just knock and ask, became obvious to Liam instead of stewing in anger.

qa.q: Why was sitting in Emeka's seat a useful step?
qa.a: It showed situational reasons on both sides: Emeka's night shifts and the hidden calendar, and Liam's own early door-banging.

qa.q: How might Emeka feel when Liam knocks with two mugs of tea?
qa.a: Emeka might feel relieved to be approached kindly, and more ready to turn the music down than if Liam had stormed in.

grounding: A student retells a conflict as a friend's story, then from the flatmate's side, and finds situational reasons for both.

passage: In the student wellness centre, the peer mentor handed Hafsa a sheet with three boxes. "Same fight, three seats," she said. In the first box Hafsa wrote it plainly: Nitin took the group's lab slot for his own experiment and didn't tell anyone. In the second, she wrote it as if it had happened to her friend Rukhsar, and was surprised how quickly she'd tell Rukhsar, "Maybe just ask him why." In the third, she sat in Nitin's chair. His supervisor had moved his submission forward by two weeks. The booking system had shown the slot as free because Hafsa hadn't confirmed it. Nitin had probably panicked. And Hafsa had been short with him in the corridor that morning, after a sleepless night. She looked at the boxes for a while, then messaged Nitin: "Coffee? I think we both had a bad week."

qa.q: What did the peer mentor hand Hafsa?
qa.a: The peer mentor handed Hafsa a sheet with three boxes.

qa.q: What did Hafsa realise when she wrote the fight as Rukhsar's?
qa.a: She was surprised how quickly she'd tell Rukhsar to just ask him why, which shows her anger had been hiding that simple idea.

qa.q: Which step helped Hafsa most, and why?
qa.a: Sitting in Nitin's chair helped most, because it showed his moved deadline and the unconfirmed booking, not just selfishness.

qa.q: How might Nitin read Hafsa's message about both having a bad week?
qa.a: Nitin may feel relieved and less defensive, since the message admits her part instead of blaming him.

grounding: A student writes a lab conflict as a friend's story and from the other student's seat, finding situational reasons on both sides.

passage:
Dear Damini,
About yesterday's shouting match over the debate schedule: I owe you a proper reply, not another angry text.
Last night I tried something. First I wrote the whole thing down as if it had happened to my cousin Shafiq. Reading it, I'd have told Shafiq, "You both want the event to work. You just want different things first."
Then I tried writing it from your chair. You'd booked the auditorium for Friday because the Wednesday slot clashes with the practical exams your whole batch has. I'd pushed for Wednesday because the visiting judges can only come then. Neither of us said our reason out loud; we just called each other stubborn.
Can we meet at the canteen at four and look at both problems together?
Tanvir

qa.q: Why had Damini booked the auditorium for Friday?
qa.a: Because the Wednesday slot clashes with the practical exams Damini's whole batch has.

qa.q: What did Tanvir realise by writing it as Shafiq's story?
qa.a: Tanvir saw that both of them wanted the event to work and just wanted different things first, which cooled the anger.

qa.q: Why is meeting at the canteen to look at both problems a good plan?
qa.a: It moves the talk from 'you're stubborn' to the real limits, the exams and the judges, which they can solve together.

qa.q: How might Damini feel reading that the exam clash was understood?
qa.a: Damini may feel respected and more willing to meet, since the letter names Damini's reason instead of calling Damini stubborn.

grounding: A student rewrites a clash as a cousin's story and then from the other person's seat, and finds the situational reasons on both sides.

passage: I'm Mariam, and I sit near the door at the travel agency, so I see who comes in when. Imran walked in at 10:25 on Tuesday, forty minutes late, rain dripping off his helmet. Usha, our manager, didn't look up. "Some people just don't take this job seriously," she said, loudly enough for him to hear. On Thursday, Usha herself came in at 10:15. "The flyover was jammed, total nightmare," she told us, and everyone nodded. I didn't say anything, but I must have glanced at Imran, because Usha followed my eyes. She went quiet. Later she called Imran in, and I heard her ask, "Tuesday, was it the rain? What's your route like?" I can't say what changed inside her. But her voice was different.

qa.q: What time did Imran walk in on Tuesday?
qa.a: Imran walked in at 10:25 on Tuesday, forty minutes late.

qa.q: What might Usha have been thinking when she went quiet?
qa.a: She may have realised she blamed Imran's attitude for his lateness but the flyover for her own.

qa.q: Why is Usha's question 'What's your route like?' a better start?
qa.a: It is curious rather than accusing, so Imran can explain the rain or his route, and any feedback can be fair.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt hearing 'Some people just don't take this job seriously'?
qa.a: Imran, still dripping from the rain, probably felt judged in front of everyone for something outside his control. 😔

grounding: A colleague watches a manager blame a late employee's attitude, excuse her own lateness by traffic, then notice and ask questions.

passage:
Monday. Tushar arrived at the clinic reception at 9:20, twenty minutes late. Ganga, the front-office manager, wrote in her notebook: "Tushar, careless attitude." She told him sharply that patients were waiting.
Wednesday. Ganga's scooter got a flat on the ring road and she walked in at 9:30. "Nothing I could do," she told the receptionist, annoyed at the tyre, not at herself. That evening, filling in her notebook, she saw Monday's line about Tushar and stopped. She had never asked him why.
The following Monday. Ganga called Tushar in before opening. "You were late last week. What happened?" He explained that the bus from his colony had been cancelled twice that month. They agreed he'd take the earlier bus and message her if it was cancelled. Her feedback note said exactly that.

qa.q: What did Ganga write in her notebook on Monday?
qa.a: She wrote, 'Tushar, careless attitude.'

qa.q: What made Ganga stop when she saw Monday's line?
qa.a: Having just blamed a flat tyre for her own lateness, she realised she had judged Tushar's attitude without ever asking why he was late.

qa.q: What did Ganga's new feedback note get right?
qa.a: It recorded the real cause, the cancelled bus, and a practical plan, instead of a label about attitude.

qa.q: What would change for Tushar if Ganga had never looked back at her notebook?
qa.a: He would still be marked as careless for cancelled buses and might feel he could never explain himself.

grounding: Over a week, a manager notices she blamed an employee's attitude for lateness but her own on a flat tyre, and makes her feedback fairer.

passage: Keerthana, you've mentioned Dinesh's late arrivals three times this evening. Let me tell you what happened to me, back when I was twenty-five, a young woman running my first shift at the garment unit. There was a tailor, Selvi, always ten minutes late. I decided she was lazy and told her so in front of everyone. One morning my bus broke down and I came in forty minutes late. I walked in blaming the bus, the road, the monsoon, and nobody questioned me. That evening my old supervisor, Mr Fernandes, laughed at me. "Ayesha, late you is unlucky, and late Selvi is lazy?" The next day I asked Selvi about her mornings. She dropped two children at two schools before work. We moved her shift by fifteen minutes. So first, ask Dinesh how his mornings go.

qa.q: How late was Ayesha on the morning the bus broke down?
qa.a: Ayesha came in forty minutes late.

qa.q: Why did young Ayesha decide Selvi was lazy?
qa.a: Ayesha only saw Selvi arrive late and never her mornings, so laziness seemed obvious, while her own lateness felt clearly the bus's fault.

qa.q: What does Ayesha want Keerthana to do about Dinesh?
qa.a: Ayesha wants Keerthana to ask Dinesh how his mornings go before judging his late arrivals.

qa.q: How might Selvi have felt being called lazy in front of everyone?
qa.a: Selvi, who was dropping two children at two schools, probably felt humiliated and unseen.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a young woman running a shift, blaming a tailor's laziness for lateness while blaming the bus for her own, and changing course.

subtype: It will not happen to me [Actor]
passage: Parveen, come down from that wall and sit here with your Vishal Dada. You think nothing will happen to you, na? I thought the same when I was nine. Behind our house in Nashik there was a mango tree, the tallest in the lane. My friend Bablu had fallen from it the summer before and broken his wrist. I told everyone, "Bablu is clumsy. I won't fall." I climbed to the thin branches where the best mangoes hung. The branch cracked, and down I came, right onto the stone step. Weeks in a plaster. Your great-grandmother fed me with her own hands and scolded me the whole time. The mangoes? Still on the tree. So, beta, climbing is fun. Just don't believe the ground makes an exception for you.

qa.q: Where was the mango tree?
qa.a: The mango tree was behind the house in Nashik, the tallest in the lane.

qa.q: Why was young Vishal sure he wouldn't fall?
qa.a: He believed Bablu fell because Bablu was clumsy, so falling felt like something that happens to other children, not to him.

qa.q: What could Parveen do to keep enjoying climbing more safely?
qa.a: Parveen could stick to strong, low branches and climb when an adult is nearby, instead of assuming a fall won't happen.

qa.q: What was the fall like for Parveen's great-grandmother?
qa.a: She had to feed Vishal with her own hands for weeks, and her scolding shows how worried she had been.

grounding: A grandfather recalls being sure, at nine, that he would not fall from a tree, because falling was for clumsier children.

passage: With Mummy away at Nani's for the week and Papa working late, nobody checked Vikas's homework. Then the class teacher announced the science test was moved to tomorrow, a whole day early. "Aren't you going to revise?" his sister Sunaina asked, stirring the dal. Vikas was lying on the floor with his comics. "Nah. Only kids like Golu fail. He never listens. I'm different." "You haven't opened the chapter on magnets." "I know magnets. Everyone knows magnets." Sunaina read out a question from his book about the poles. Vikas guessed wrong, laughed, and said the real test wouldn't ask that. The power went off at nine, and he fell asleep happily in the dark, completely sure tomorrow would go fine. Sunaina lay awake worrying for both of them.

qa.a: The science test was moved to tomorrow, a whole day early.

qa.q: Why is Vikas so relaxed about the test?
qa.a: He believes only kids like Golu fail, so a bad result feels like something that happens to others, not to him.

qa.q: What small step could help Vikas before the test?

passage: Behind Kunal's building in Andheri stood a half-built tower with a torn blue sheet over the fence. Every evening, the guard shooed kids away. "We'll cut through and reach the park in two minutes," Kunal told Samir. "That guard caught Tinku last week," said Samir. "Tinku is slow. The guard won't catch me." "You've never gone in." "Exactly. So he's never caught me." Samir laughed, but his feet didn't move. Kunal ducked under the sheet, stepped over a pile of iron rods and sprinted toward the far gap. The guard's whistle shrieked. Two minutes later Kunal was standing at the guard's cabin while his father's phone number was written in a register, and Samir waited on the footpath outside.

qa.q: What happened after the guard's whistle shrieked?
qa.a: Kunal was standing at the guard's cabin while his father's phone number was written in a register.

qa.q: Why was Kunal so sure the guard wouldn't catch him?
qa.a: He saw Tinku as slow and himself as different, so getting caught felt like something that only happens to other kids.

qa.q: What could Kunal have asked himself before ducking under the sheet?
qa.a: He could have asked, 'Why would I be luckier than Tinku?' and taken the longer road to the park with Samir.

qa.q: Why might Samir have reacted differently to the shortcut?
qa.a: Samir took Tinku getting caught as a real warning, so his feet didn't move while Kunal went in.

grounding: A boy is sure a guard will not catch him because being caught is for slower kids, and gets caught.

passage:
"Harish, helmet!" Parul held it out at the gate.
"Didi, it's two minutes on the cycle to tuition."
"Two minutes is enough."
"It squashes my hair. Nobody wears one for short rides."
"Remember Sunny from B-block? Short ride too."
"Sunny was showing off. I ride properly."
"And the auto that took the turn without looking? Was Sunny showing off then?"
"Didi, relax. Nothing's going to happen to me."
"That's exactly what Sunny said."
Harish grinned and pushed off the kerb. "I'm different."
Parul didn't smile. She stood in front of the cycle, holding the helmet out, until he sighed, snatched it and jammed it on.

qa.q: Why does Harish say he doesn't need the helmet?
qa.a: He says it's two minutes on the cycle to tuition and the helmet squashes his hair.

qa.q: Why does Harish feel that nothing is going to happen to him?
qa.a: He tells himself Sunny was showing off and he rides properly, so harm feels like it belongs to others, while the comfort of no helmet is right now.

qa.q: Which of Parul's moves worked, and why?
qa.a: Standing calmly in front of the cycle worked better than more arguing, because it kept the choice in front of him and let him give in without a fight.

qa.q: What is it like for Parul to watch Harish push off without a helmet?
qa.a: Parul remembers what happened to Sunny, so she feels a real fear that he doesn't, which is why she didn't smile.

grounding: A teenager insists he won't get hurt riding without a helmet, seeing accidents as something for other riders.

passage: I'm Amandeep, and I'm writing this a few months after the thing with Jatin's vape. It started in Class 10, behind the school water tank. Jatin had a flavoured one, mango, and passed it around. I knew the posters in the corridor said it was harmful. But in my head those posters were about other people, adults who'd smoked for twenty years, not a sixteen-year-old taking a few puffs. The sweet taste and everyone laughing felt huge right then; 'later' felt like a made-up word. Within weeks Jatin was sneaking out between classes, and irritable when he couldn't. That scared me more than any poster. I stopped going to the water tank, and I told my older cousin, who helped Jatin talk to the school counsellor.

qa.q: Where did it start?
qa.a: It started in Class 10, behind the school water tank.

qa.q: Why didn't the corridor posters feel like they applied to Amandeep?
qa.a: Amandeep thought they were about other people who had smoked for years, and the sweet taste and laughter right then felt much bigger than 'later'.

qa.q: What did Amandeep do that was wise?
qa.a: Amandeep stepped away from the water tank and told an older cousin, who helped Jatin reach the school counsellor.

qa.q: How did Jatin's changes affect Amandeep?
qa.a: Seeing Jatin sneak out between classes and turn irritable scared Amandeep more than any poster, and made the harm real.

grounding: A teenager recalls believing vaping harms only other people, while the immediate buzz outweighed any thought of later.

passage:
Note from Coach Trisha, district swimming camp, day 4
This afternoon Ojas and two older boys slipped away to the old quarry pond behind the camp. There's a board there saying the water is deep and cold. When I found them, Ojas was on the ledge, ready to jump. He said, laughing, "Coach, I'm the strongest swimmer here. Those warnings are for people who can't swim." He seemed to truly believe it. The rush of the jump was all he could see.
I didn't shout. I sat with him on the bank and asked who he thought the board was written for. He shrugged. I told him strong swimmers get cramps in cold water too.
Next steps: told the camp head and called his parents this evening. Tomorrow the whole group walks to the quarry with the lifeguard to hear about the risks on site.

qa.q: What does the board at the quarry pond say?
qa.a: The board says the water is deep and cold.

qa.q: What does Ojas's laughing reply suggest about how he sees the danger?
qa.a: It suggests he truly feels the warning is for weaker swimmers, and the rush of the jump outweighs any thought of harm.

qa.q: How did Coach Trisha respond without lecturing?
qa.a: Coach Trisha sat with him, asked who the board was for, told the camp head and his parents the same day, and planned a site visit with the lifeguard.

qa.q: How might Ojas's parents feel when they hear about the quarry?
qa.a: They would likely feel scared, and grateful the coach found him in time.

grounding: A coach records a strong teenage swimmer believing a danger sign is only for weaker people, and the calm steps taken.

passage:
May. Rashmi had one application out, to the design studio everyone admired. "They'll take me, I'm top of the batch," she told her brother Yash, and bought an expensive drawing tablet on instalments. When Yash asked about other applications, she laughed. "Backups are for people who expect to fail."
July. An email arrived: the studio had frozen all hiring for the year. Rashmi sat on the balcony for a long time, the instalment reminder blinking on her phone. She hadn't applied anywhere else, and her savings were a few thousand rupees.
September. Rashmi kept a spreadsheet now: fourteen applications, two interviews, one freelance project slowly paying off the tablet. Yash helped her practise answers every Sunday. "Still aiming for the dream studio?" he asked. "Next year," she said. "With a second route this time."

qa.q: What did the studio's email say in July?
qa.a: The studio had frozen all hiring for the year.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi feel no need for other applications in May?
qa.a: Being top of the batch made her sure she'd be chosen, so backups felt like expecting to fail.

qa.q: What changed in Rashmi's approach by September that helps?
qa.a: She spread her chances with fourteen applications and freelance work while still aiming for the dream studio, so her hope now has a plan under it.

qa.q: How might Yash have felt watching Rashmi on the balcony in July?
qa.a: Yash, who had asked about other applications, probably felt worried and sorry for her rather than smug.

grounding: A graduate bets everything on one dream job and skips backups until a hiring freeze shows how fragile unprepared hope is.

passage: Himani, you're moving to Bengaluru next month and you keep saying everything will fall into place. It might. Let your Sarita Maasi tell you how it went for me. At twenty-two I got my first job in Delhi and decided my life would go better than everyone's. My salary would rise every year, my boyfriend and I would marry by twenty-five, and I'd start saving later. So I spent every rupee. Then the company shut down in my second year. No savings, rent due, and the boyfriend moved to Pune without much of a goodbye. I came home to your Nani with one suitcase and a lot of pride to swallow. Hope isn't the problem, beta. Hope with nothing under it is. Keep a little aside, and keep a second door open.

qa.q: Where did Sarita get her first job?
qa.a: Sarita got her first job in Delhi at twenty-two.

qa.q: Why did young Sarita spend every rupee?
qa.a: She felt sure her life would go better than everyone's, with pay rises and marriage on schedule, so saving seemed like something for later.

qa.q: What is Sarita Maasi asking Himani to do, in practice?
qa.a: To keep Himani's hope for Bengaluru but put a little aside and keep a second option open in case things go wrong.

qa.q: How might Himani hear this story just before her move?
qa.a: Himani may feel a little deflated at first, but also cared for, since Sarita Maasi is sharing an embarrassing memory to protect her.

grounding: An aunt recalls expecting her first job, money and relationship to go better than average and having nothing ready when they failed.

passage: Chetan signed the lease on the one-bedroom flat in Kochi before his offer letter had even arrived. "The interview went brilliantly. They practically hired me on the spot," he told Leela, his girlfriend, as they carried his mattress up three flights of stairs. Leela asked, gently, whether he'd kept any other interviews going. "Why would I? This one's done." The landlord wanted two months' deposit by Friday, and Chetan paid it with the money his parents had given for the convocation trip. On Thursday, the offer letter came: the joining date had been pushed back three months. Chetan sat on the bare mattress in the empty flat, rent due in four weeks, phone in hand, and realised he didn't have a single other lead.

qa.q: What did the offer letter say?
qa.a: The joining date had been pushed back three months.

qa.q: Why didn't Chetan keep other interviews going?
qa.a: The interview felt so good that he was sure the job was certain, so other options seemed pointless.

qa.q: What could Chetan do now, sitting on the mattress?
qa.a: He could restart applications right away and talk honestly with his parents about the gap, instead of hoping the date moves back.

qa.q: How might Leela feel remembering her gentle question?
qa.a: Leela may feel sad for him rather than proved right, since she had quietly hoped he'd keep a backup.

grounding: A graduate commits to a flat and deposit on the strength of one interview and has no fallback when the job is delayed.

passage: Beatriz had been baking custard tarts in her Porto kitchen since five, humming. Her weekend market stall opened in two weeks, and she believed in it completely. Still, on the fridge hung a list her friend Lindiwe had teased her about: "Three months of rent put aside. Two cafés who'd take wholesale orders. Stall date plus two weeks, just in case." On Tuesday the council emailed: the market would close for a month for repairs. Lindiwe came round expecting tears. Instead Beatriz was on the phone to the first café. "It's a delay, not a verdict," she said, sliding a tray into the oven. "The tarts are still good. I'm still good. The plan just moves." By evening, one café had ordered forty tarts for Saturday.

qa.q: Why was the market closing?
qa.a: The market would close for a month for repairs.

qa.q: What does 'It's a delay, not a verdict' show about how Beatriz sees the setback?
qa.a: It shows the closure hit her plan, not her belief in herself or her tarts, so she can stay hopeful and act. 🙂

qa.q: Which part of Beatriz's preparation helped most, and why?
qa.a: The café idea on the fridge list helped most, because it gave her a ready second route she could call the same day.

qa.q: How does Lindiwe's view of the list change?
qa.a: Lindiwe teased her about the list and came expecting tears, but then watched it turn a closure into a Saturday order.

grounding: A hopeful young baker keeps savings, backup buyers and a time buffer, so a market closure hits her plan but not her sense of self.

passage: In the NGO's cramped office above a pharmacy, Meenal pinned her plan for the children's reading festival on the wall. Siddharth read it and raised an eyebrow. "You've got a whole column called 'If this fails'." "I expect it to go brilliantly," Meenal said. "That's why I'll work nights on it. But the school hall is booked for a backup date, a tenth of the budget is kept for surprises, and the storyteller has a stand-in." Three weeks later, the main sponsor cut its money by half, two days before the event. Pradeep, the director, came in looking grim. Meenal had already opened her 'If this fails' column. The surprise money covered the printing, and the book stall moved into the free school hall. "Annoying," she said, crossing out a line. "But it's the plan that took the hit. Not me."

qa.q: What was the column on Meenal's plan called?
qa.a: The column was called 'If this fails'.

qa.q: How can you tell Meenal is still hopeful about the festival?
qa.a: She says she expects it to go brilliantly and will work nights on it, so the backup column is preparation, not doubt.

qa.q: What could other planners borrow from Meenal's approach?
qa.a: Keep a backup date or venue, set aside part of the budget for surprises, and decide the fallback before trouble starts.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel when he sees Meenal already handling it?
qa.a: Pradeep came in grim, so Pradeep would likely feel relief and more trust in Meenal's planning.

grounding: An NGO planner stays hopeful but builds a backup date, a surprise fund and a fallback, so a sponsor cut hits the plan and not her.

passage:
Dear Lalit,
You asked how I stay so calm about the film course in Chennai. Honestly, I'm excited. I think I'll get in, and I'm working like I will: portfolio done, two short films shot.
But here's what I didn't tell you. I've applied to two other courses too, one online. I've kept four months of expenses in a separate account I don't touch. And I told Santosh sir at the studio I could keep editing part-time if the course is delayed.
Yesterday it was. The institute moved admissions to next year.
I cried for about ten minutes. Then I opened my list and called Santosh sir. I start part-time on Monday, and my portfolio gets one more year to grow.
The course said "not yet". It didn't say "not you".
Your big sister,
Kaveri

qa.q: What did the institute do yesterday?
qa.a: The institute moved admissions to next year.

qa.q: What does 'It didn't say not you' show about Kaveri's feelings?
qa.a: It shows Kaveri was sad but saw the delay as a setback to her plan, not a judgement on her worth.

qa.q: What made Kaveri's quick recovery possible?
qa.a: Her backups were ready before the news: two other applications, four months of expenses set aside, and part-time editing with Santosh sir.

qa.q: How might Lalit see Kaveri's calm after this letter?
qa.a: Lalit might realise her calm comes from quiet preparation, not luck, and feel proud of her. 🤍

grounding: A young woman stays hopeful about a film course while keeping other applications, savings and part-time work ready, so a delay doesn't shake her.
